SSRI-related sexual dysfunction

One case report describes partial recovery of penile sensation after low-power laser treatment. Anejaculation and erectile difficulties did not improve.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Penile sensation — Waldinger et al. 2015 reported patient-estimated partial recovery after 20 sessions: about 20% of pre-paroxetine sensitivity when erect and 40% when flaccid. Anejaculation and erectile difficulties remained unchanged. This is an uncontrolled single-case observation.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low certainty for partial penile-sensation recovery after PBM in one post-SSRI case (Waldinger et al. 2015).

Summary of the Evidence

One case report describes partial improvement in penile sensation after low-power laser treatment for persistent post-SSRI sexual dysfunction. Anejaculation and erectile difficulties remained unchanged.

Human and clinical evidence

The report concerns a man whose sensory and sexual symptoms began during paroxetine treatment and persisted after the medicine was stopped. After 20 laser sessions, he reported partial return of penile touch and temperature sensation. The reported change was about 20% of pre-paroxetine sensitivity when erect and 40% when flaccid; anejaculation and erectile difficulties did not improve (Waldinger et al. 2015).

Animal evidence

No animal study specifically addressing post-SSRI sexual dysfunction was identified.

Literature synthesis

A 2022 comprehensive narrative review considered transcranial PBM for sexual dysfunction related to depression or antidepressant medication. It did not test genital PBM for post-SSRI sexual dysfunction and reported no pooled effect estimate (Salehpour et al. 2022).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The case report describes 20 sessions of 15 minutes using single- and multi-diode pulsed low-power laser probes directed to genital tissue. The database lists a wavelength near 900 nm, but the delivered dose and other details needed to reproduce treatment were not specified adequately. This single case cannot show whether other people with post-SSRI symptoms would respond.

Interpretation

The report is a clinical observation of partial sensory change, not controlled evidence that PBM treats post-SSRI sexual dysfunction. The persistent ejaculation and erection problems show that outcomes differed within this case. Prospective assessment with objective sensory testing, validated sexual-function measures, adverse-event monitoring, and a comparator would be needed to evaluate this possible treatment.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The only directly relevant treatment report describes partial sensory change in one person and persistent ejaculation and erection problems (Waldinger et al. 2015). There was no control group, objective sensory testing, or independent replication. The related 2022 review concerns transcranial PBM and does not add controlled evidence for genital treatment (Salehpour et al. 2022).
